newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG leader faces new threat in political crisis.
newsitem.headline: PNG leader faces new threat in political crisis.

text.p: The prime minister of Papua New Guinea, Sir Julius Chan, came under further political pressure on Monday when the country's effective head of state urged him to step aside.

Sir Wiwa Korowi called an emergency meeting of senior officials, on the eve of a parliamentary motion seeking Chan's resignation, to discuss the stand-off between Chan and his political and military opponents.

Korowi said Chan should stand aside pending the outcome of an inquiry into a contract signed between the government and a company which provided mercenaries which the government hoped to use to help crush a rebellion on Bougainville island.
"He should stand aside temporarily, pending the outcome of the inquiry," Korowi told reporters after the meeting.
"If there is no compromise reached between now and tomorrow (Tuesday), and the hours are ticking away, we have to find something to cool it off," he said.
Korowi has no powers to sack Chan but as the representative of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, the country's titular head of state under Commonwealth protocol, he has considerable political influence.
Rebel army officers have also set Chan a deadline to quit by Tuesday over the $36 million contract with British mercenary company Sandline International that ended up as a fiasco.
The British commander of the mercenaries, retired colonel Tim Spicer, appeared in court on Monday and pleaded not guilty to two illegal firearm charges.
Ahead of Tuesday's vote, parliament became a focal point for anti-government protest.
About 150 demonstrators sat outside the building, carrying banners proclaiming "Chan, you have jeopardised democracy" and "Hallelujiah, 21 years of corruption is coming to an end".
A small number of police watched them calmly.
"There will be more of us tomorrow, tens of thousands more," said protest leader Jonathon O'Ata.
"Tomorrow's the deadline and if it doesn't fall favourably for the people, there could be violence," he said.
The contract with British-based Sandline International sparked the worst political crisis in the nation's 22 years of independence when army chief Jerry Singirok demanded Chan quit over the deal.
Singirok was sacked and the capital, Port Moresby, was rocked by two days of violent demonstrations.
Korowi, saying there was no need yet for Chan to resign completely, pleaded to both sides for compromise to prevent plunging this impverished nation into further turmoil.

In what diplomats saw as a move to appease his rebellious military, Chan late on Sunday replaced acting defence chief Colonel Alfred Aikung with Singirok's deputy, Colonel Jack Tuat, who is seen as a Singirok ally.

Singirok on Monday appealed to the army to unite behind Tuat. "I am not the Messiah, I am only the instrument," the popular sacked commander told troops at Murray Barracks, where they have been holed up since the trouble started.
"It's beyond me now. The parliament sits tomorrow, whatever transpires from there, it's political. That's the democratic process that I am talking about. It's the people's call."
The week-long crisis has preoccupied Papua New Guinea's Pacific neighbours.
Australia, its former colonial power, has had troops on standby to help around 10,000 Australian nationals who live in the country if the situation deteriorates.
New Zealand also said on Monday that it was working on contingency plans to evacuate its nationals.
Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said that although New Zealand had to be prepared to act, relative calm appeared to be holding and there was no immediate concern for people's safety.
"Obviously people are doing some work on this at the present time though I'm not aware that we have lifted to the same level of alert that the Australians have," McKinnon said.
